   \[\Delta L=\frac{(9.6\times10^3)(15)}{(8.0\times10^{-5})(2.0\times10^{11})}\,\text{m}\]
   Denominator:
   \[(8.0\times10^{-5})(2.0\times10^{11})=1.6\times10^7\]
   \[\Delta L=\frac{1.44\times10^5}{1.6\times10^7}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L=9.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Working stress:
   \[\sigma_w=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{9.6\times10^3}{8.0\times10^{-5}}\,\text{Pa}\]
   \[\sigma_w=1.2\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\]
   Factor of safety:
   \[n=\frac{6.0\times10^8}{1.2\times10^8}=5\]
   The acceleration direction changes the cable tension before any stress or extension calculation is made.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(9.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\) and \(5\).

question: A composite wire has two segments in series. Segment \(P\) has \(L_1=1.0\,\text{m}\), \(A_1=2.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), and \(Y_1=1.2\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\). Segment \(Q\) has \(L_2=1.5\,\text{m}\), \(A_2=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), and \(Y_2=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\). A load of \(240\,\text{N}\) is gradually applied. The total extension and stored energy are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Series condition:} \) The same load \(F=240\,\text{N}\) acts through both segments.
   Segment \(P\) extension:
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{FL_1}{A_1Y_1}\]
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{(240)(1.0)}{(2.0\times10^{-6})(1.2\times10^{11})}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{240}{2.4\times10^5}=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Segment \(Q\) extension:
   \[\Delta L_2=\frac{FL_2}{A_2Y_2}\]
   \[\Delta L_2=\frac{(240)(1.5)}{(1.0\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L_2=\frac{360}{2.0\times10^5}=1.8\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Total extension:
   \[\Delta L=\Delta L_1+\Delta L_2\]
   \[\Delta L=2.8\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Stored elastic energy:
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}F\Delta L\]
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}(240)(2.8\times10^{-3})\,\text{J}\]
   \[U=0.336\,\text{J}\]
   The softer or thinner segment contributes more to total extension even though the same force passes through both.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(2.8\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\) and \(0.336\,\text{J}\).

question: An isotropic material has \(B=1.5\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\) and \(G=6.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\). Using \(Y=\frac{9BG}{3B+G}\) and \(Y=2G(1+\nu)\), its Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio are closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known data:} \) \(B=1.5\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\) and \(G=6.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\).
   Use:
   \[Y=\frac{9BG}{3B+G}\]
   Denominator:
   \[3B+G=3(1.5\times10^{11})+6.0\times10^{10}\]
   \[3B+G=4.5\times10^{11}+0.6\times10^{11}=5.1\times10^{11}\]
   Numerator:
   \[9BG=9(1.5\times10^{11})(6.0\times10^{10})\]
   \[9BG=81\times10^{21}=8.1\times10^{22}\]
   Therefore:
   \[Y=\frac{8.1\times10^{22}}{5.1\times10^{11}}\,\text{Pa}\]
   \[Y\approx1.59\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\]
   Now use:
   \[Y=2G(1+\nu)\]
   \[\nu=\frac{Y}{2G}-1\]
   \[\nu=\frac{1.59\times10^{11}}{2(6.0\times10^{10})}-1\]
   \[\nu\approx1.324-1=0.324\]
   Both relations are valid here only because the material is stated to be isotropic.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(1.59\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\) and \(0.324\).

question: A rod of area \(4.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}^2\), \(Y=1.5\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), and \(\alpha=1.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{K}^{-1}\) is heated by \(50\,\text{K}\). Only \(80\%\) of the free expansion is prevented. An external tensile force of \(1000\,\text{N}\) is also applied. The resultant stress is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Thermal part:} \) Free thermal strain would be:
   \[\epsilon_{\text{free}}=\alpha\Delta T\]
   \[\epsilon_{\text{free}}=(1.0\times10^{-5})(50)=5.0\times10^{-4}\]
   Since \(80\%\) is prevented:
   \[\epsilon_{\text{prevented}}=0.80(5.0\times10^{-4})=4.0\times10^{-4}\]
   Thermal stress:
   \[\sigma_{\text{th}}=Y\epsilon_{\text{prevented}}\]
   \[\sigma_{\text{th}}=(1.5\times10^{11})(4.0\times10^{-4})\]
   \[\sigma_{\text{th}}=6.0\times10^7\,\text{Pa}\]
   This thermal stress is compressive because heating expansion is opposed.
   \( \textbf{External stress:} \)
   \[\sigma_{\text{ext}}=\frac{F}{A}\]
   \[\sigma_{\text{ext}}=\frac{1000}{4.0\times10^{-5}}=2.5\times10^7\,\text{Pa}\]
   This stress is tensile.
   Net stress, taking tensile positive:
   \[\sigma_{\text{net}}=+2.5\times10^7-6.0\times10^7\]
   \[\sigma_{\text{net}}=-3.5\times10^7\,\text{Pa}\]
   The resultant is compressive because the prevented thermal expansion dominates the applied pull.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(3.5\times10^7\,\text{Pa}\), compressive.

question: A wire has a straight load-extension graph with slope \(5.0\times10^4\,\text{N m}^{-1}\). Its length is \(2.0\,\text{m}\) and radius is \(0.50\,\text{mm}\). Taking \(\pi=3.14\), the Young’s modulus and the energy stored at extension \(1.5\,\text{mm}\) are closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known data:} \) Load-extension slope \(k=5.0\times10^4\,\text{N m}^{-1}\), \(L=2.0\,\text{m}\), and \(r=0.50\,\text{mm}=5.0\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}\).
   Area:
   \[A=\pi r^2\]
   \[A=3.14(5.0\times10^{-4})^2\]
   \[A=7.85\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}^2\]
   For a wire:
   \[k=\frac{AY}{L}\]
   \[Y=\frac{kL}{A}\]
   \[Y=\frac{(5.0\times10^4)(2.0)}{7.85\times10^{-7}}\,\text{Pa}\]
   \[Y\approx1.27\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\]
   At extension:
   \[\Delta L=1.5\,\text{mm}=1.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Energy stored in a linear graph:
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}k(\Delta L)^2\]
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}(5.0\times10^4)(1.5\times10^{-3})^2\,\text{J}\]
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}(5.0\times10^4)(2.25\times10^{-6})\]
   \[U=5.625\times10^{-2}\,\text{J}\]
   The graph slope gives wire stiffness first, not Young’s modulus until \(L\) and \(A\) are included.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(1.27\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\) and \(5.63\times10^{-2}\,\text{J}\).

question: A solid of volume \(2.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3\) decreases in volume by \(5.0\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}^3\) when pressure is increased by \(1.0\times10^7\,\text{Pa}\). Its bulk modulus and compressibility are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known data:} \) \(V=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3\), \(\Delta V=-5.0\times10^{-7}\,\text{m}^3\), and \(\Delta P=1.0\times10^7\,\text{Pa}\).
   First calculate the magnitude of volumetric strain:
   \[\frac{|\Delta V|}{V}=\frac{5.0\times10^{-7}}{2.0\times10^{-3}}\]
   \[\frac{|\Delta V|}{V}=2.5\times10^{-4}\]
   Bulk modulus:
   \[B=\frac{\Delta P}{|\Delta V|/V}\]
   \[B=\frac{1.0\times10^7}{2.5\times10^{-4}}\,\text{Pa}\]
   \[B=4.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\]
   Compressibility:
   \[K_c=\frac{1}{B}\]
   \[K_c=\frac{1}{4.0\times10^{10}}\,\text{Pa}^{-1}\]
   \[K_c=2.5\times10^{-11}\,\text{Pa}^{-1}\]
   The smaller the fractional volume change for a pressure rise, the larger the bulk modulus and the smaller the compressibility.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(4.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\) and \(2.5\times10^{-11}\,\text{Pa}^{-1}\).

question: A cable must carry \(1.5\times10^4\,\text{N}\), has length \(10\,\text{m}\), \(Y=1.5\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), breaking stress \(9.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\), and required factor of safety \(3\). Its extension must not exceed \(4.0\,\text{mm}\). Taking \(\pi=3.14\), the controlling condition and minimum radius are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Strength condition:} \) Safe working stress:
   \[\sigma_w=\frac{9.0\times10^8}{3}=3.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\]
   Area needed by strength:
   \[A_1=\frac{F}{\sigma_w}\]
   \[A_1=\frac{1.5\times10^4}{3.0\times10^8}\,\text{m}^2\]
   \[A_1=5.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}^2\]
   \( \textbf{Extension condition:} \)
   \[\Delta L_{\max}=4.0\,\text{mm}=4.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L=\frac{FL}{AY}\]
   \[A_2=\frac{FL}{Y\Delta L_{\max}}\]
   \[A_2=\frac{(1.5\times10^4)(10)}{(1.5\times10^{11})(4.0\times10^{-3})}\,\text{m}^2\]
   \[A_2=\frac{1.5\times10^5}{6.0\times10^8}\,\text{m}^2\]
   \[A_2=2.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2\]
   Since \(A_2 \gt A_1\), the extension condition controls the design.
   Radius from \(A=\pi r^2\):
   \[r=\sqrt{\frac{A_2}{\pi}}\]
   \[r=\sqrt{\frac{2.5\times10^{-4}}{3.14}}\,\text{m}\]
   \[r\approx8.92\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) extension condition, \(8.92\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).

question: A wire is under tensile stress \(2.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\). Its \(Y=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), \(\nu=0.30\), and initial volume is \(1.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3\). Using \(\epsilon_V\approx\epsilon_L+2\epsilon_{\text{lat}}\), the total elastic energy and approximate volume change are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known data:} \) \(\sigma=2.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\), \(Y=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), \(\nu=0.30\), and \(V=1.0\times10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3\).
   Longitudinal strain:
   \[\epsilon_L=\frac{\sigma}{Y}\]
   \[\epsilon_L=\frac{2.0\times10^8}{2.0\times10^{11}}=1.0\times10^{-3}\]
   Lateral strain:
   \[\epsilon_{\text{lat}}=-\nu\epsilon_L\]
   \[\epsilon_{\text{lat}}=-(0.30)(1.0\times10^{-3})=-3.0\times10^{-4}\]
   Approximate volume strain:
   \[\epsilon_V\approx\epsilon_L+2\epsilon_{\text{lat}}\]
   \[\epsilon_V=1.0\times10^{-3}+2(-3.0\times10^{-4})\]
   \[\epsilon_V=4.0\times10^{-4}\]
   Volume change:
   \[\Delta V=\epsilon_VV=(4.0\times10^{-4})(1.0\times10^{-5})\,\text{m}^3\]
   \[\Delta V=4.0\times10^{-9}\,\text{m}^3\]
   Energy density:
   \[u=\frac{1}{2}\sigma\epsilon_L\]
   \[u=\frac{1}{2}(2.0\times10^8)(1.0\times10^{-3})=1.0\times10^5\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   Total energy:
   \[U=uV=(1.0\times10^5)(1.0\times10^{-5})=1.0\,\text{J}\]
   The same longitudinal strain is used once for energy and once with Poisson’s ratio for volume change.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(1.0\,\text{J}\) and \(4.0\times10^{-9}\,\text{m}^3\).

question: A block of height \(0.10\,\text{m}\), top-face area \(2.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2\), and shear modulus \(4.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\) is acted on by a tangential force of \(4000\,\text{N}\). The shearing strain, sideways displacement, and elastic energy stored are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Known data:} \) \(L=0.10\,\text{m}\), \(A=2.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^2\), \(G=4.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\), and \(F=4000\,\text{N}\).
   Shearing stress:
   \[\tau=\frac{F}{A}\]
   \[\tau=\frac{4000}{2.0\times10^{-3}}\,\text{Pa}\]
   \[\tau=2.0\times10^6\,\text{Pa}\]
   Shearing strain:
   \[\gamma=\frac{\tau}{G}\]
   \[\gamma=\frac{2.0\times10^6}{4.0\times10^{10}}\]
   \[\gamma=5.0\times10^{-5}\]
   Sideways displacement:
   \[\gamma=\frac{\Delta x}{L}\]
   \[\Delta x=\gamma L=(5.0\times10^{-5})(0.10)\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta x=5.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}\]
   Elastic energy in shear:
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}F\Delta x\]
   \[U=\frac{1}{2}(4000)(5.0\times10^{-6})\,\text{J}\]
   \[U=1.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{J}\]
   The force first gives stress, stress gives strain, and strain gives displacement.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(5.0\times10^{-5}\), \(5.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}\), and \(1.0\times10^{-2}\,\text{J}\).

question: A small solid sample of volume \(1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3\) is separately compressed and sheared within the elastic range. In compression, \(\Delta P=3.0\times10^6\,\text{Pa}\) and \(B=9.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\). In shear, \(\tau=2.0\times10^6\,\text{Pa}\) and \(G=5.0\times10^{10}\,\text{Pa}\). The total elastic energy density from these two independent deformations is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Compression energy density:} \) For linear bulk compression:
   \[u_B=\frac{(\Delta P)^2}{2B}\]
   Substitute:
   \[u_B=\frac{(3.0\times10^6)^2}{2(9.0\times10^{10})}\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   \[u_B=\frac{9.0\times10^{12}}{1.8\times10^{11}}\]
   \[u_B=50\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   \( \textbf{Shear energy density:} \)
   \[u_G=\frac{\tau^2}{2G}\]
   \[u_G=\frac{(2.0\times10^6)^2}{2(5.0\times10^{10})}\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   \[u_G=\frac{4.0\times10^{12}}{1.0\times10^{11}}\]
   \[u_G=40\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   Total energy density:
   \[u=u_B+u_G\]
   \[u=50+40=90\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   The two energy densities can be added because the compression and shear data are treated as independent elastic contributions.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(90\,\text{J m}^{-3}\).

question: Two wires are fixed in parallel between the same supports and carry a total load of \(900\,\text{N}\). Wire \(P\) has \(L_1=1.0\,\text{m}\), \(A_1=2.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(Y_1=1.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\). Wire \(Q\) has \(L_2=2.0\,\text{m}\), \(A_2=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(Y_2=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\). The common extension and loads in \(P\) and \(Q\) are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Parallel condition:} \) Both wires have the same extension \(\Delta L\).
   Wire stiffness is:
   \[k=\frac{AY}{L}\]
   For wire \(P\):
   \[k_1=\frac{(2.0\times10^{-6})(1.0\times10^{11})}{1.0}\]
   \[k_1=2.0\times10^5\,\text{N m}^{-1}\]
   For wire \(Q\):
   \[k_2=\frac{(1.0\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})}{2.0}\]
   \[k_2=1.0\times10^5\,\text{N m}^{-1}\]
   Total stiffness:
   \[k=k_1+k_2=3.0\times10^5\,\text{N m}^{-1}\]
   Common extension:
   \[\Delta L=\frac{900}{3.0\times10^5}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L=3.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Load carried by \(P\):
   \[F_1=k_1\Delta L=(2.0\times10^5)(3.0\times10^{-3})=600\,\text{N}\]
   Load carried by \(Q\):
   \[F_2=k_2\Delta L=(1.0\times10^5)(3.0\times10^{-3})=300\,\text{N}\]
   The stiffer wire takes the larger share of the load.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(3.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), \(600\,\text{N}\), and \(300\,\text{N}\).

question: Two segments are joined in series to form a cable. Segment \(P\) has \(A_1=2.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(L_1=1.0\,\text{m}\), \(Y_1=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), and breaking stress \(5.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\). Segment \(Q\) has \(A_2=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(L_2=2.0\,\text{m}\), \(Y_2=1.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), and breaking stress \(8.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\). If the factor of safety is \(2\), the maximum safe load and total extension at that load are
explanation:
\( \textbf{Safe load for segment \(P\):} \)
   \[F_{P,\text{safe}}=\frac{\sigma_{bP}A_1}{n}\]
   \[F_{P,\text{safe}}=\frac{(5.0\times10^8)(2.0\times10^{-6})}{2}\,\text{N}\]
   \[F_{P,\text{safe}}=500\,\text{N}\]
   \( \textbf{Safe load for segment \(Q\):} \)
   \[F_{Q,\text{safe}}=\frac{\sigma_{bQ}A_2}{n}\]
   \[F_{Q,\text{safe}}=\frac{(8.0\times10^8)(1.0\times10^{-6})}{2}\,\text{N}\]
   \[F_{Q,\text{safe}}=400\,\text{N}\]
   The series cable is limited by the weaker safe-load segment, so:
   \[F_{\text{safe}}=400\,\text{N}\]
   Extension of \(P\):
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{FL_1}{A_1Y_1}\]
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{(400)(1.0)}{(2.0\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L_1=1.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Extension of \(Q\):
   \[\Delta L_2=\frac{FL_2}{A_2Y_2}\]
   \[\Delta L_2=\frac{(400)(2.0)}{(1.0\times10^{-6})(1.0\times10^{11})}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L_2=8.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   Total extension:
   \[\Delta L=9.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\]
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(400\,\text{N}\) and \(9.0\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\).

question: A wire has stress \(1.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\) and strain \(4.0\times10^{-4}\) at a certain point in the linear elastic region. Its volume is \(6.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^3\). If the stress is increased to \(2.5\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\) without leaving the linear region, the new total elastic energy stored is
explanation:
\( \textbf{First find Young’s modulus:} \)
   \[Y=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon}\]
   \[Y=\frac{1.0\times10^8}{4.0\times10^{-4}}\,\text{Pa}\]
   \[Y=2.5\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\]
   New stress:
   \[\sigma_2=2.5\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\]
   Energy density in terms of stress:
   \[u=\frac{\sigma^2}{2Y}\]
   Substitute the new stress:
   \[u_2=\frac{(2.5\times10^8)^2}{2(2.5\times10^{11})}\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   \[(2.5\times10^8)^2=6.25\times10^{16}\]
   \[2Y=5.0\times10^{11}\]
   \[u_2=\frac{6.25\times10^{16}}{5.0\times10^{11}}\]
   \[u_2=1.25\times10^5\,\text{J m}^{-3}\]
   Total energy:
   \[U=u_2V\]
   \[U=(1.25\times10^5)(6.0\times10^{-6})\,\text{J}\]
   \[U=0.75\,\text{J}\]
   The energy rises with the square of stress, so the new stored energy is not found by a simple stress ratio alone unless that square dependence is included.
   \( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(0.75\,\text{J}\).

question: Two wires of equal length \(2.0\,\text{m}\) are fixed in parallel between the same supports and share a load. Wire \(P\) has \(A_1=1.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(Y_1=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), and breaking stress \(6.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\). Wire \(Q\) has \(A_2=2.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(Y_2=1.5\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), and breaking stress \(4.5\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\). If the factor of safety is \(3\) for both wires and the common extension must not exceed \(1.5\,\text{mm}\), the maximum total load is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Parallel condition:} \) Both wires have the same extension \(\Delta L\).
   The stiffness of a wire is:
   \[k=\frac{AY}{L}\]
   For wire \(P\):
   \[k_1=\frac{(1.0\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})}{2.0}=1.0\times10^5\,\text{N m}^{-1}\]

question: A composite cable has two segments in series. Segment \(P\) has \(L_1=1.5\,\text{m}\), \(A_1=2.0\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\), \(Y_1=2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{Pa}\), and breaking stress \(7.0\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\). explanation:
\( \textbf{Series condition:} \) The same tensile force passes through both segments.
   Safe stress for segment \(P\):
   \[\sigma_{w1}=\frac{7.0\times10^8}{3}=2.333\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\]
   Safe load for segment \(P\):
   \[F_{1,\max}=\sigma_{w1}A_1\]
   \[F_{1,\max}=(2.333\times10^8)(2.0\times10^{-6})\,\text{N}\]
   \[F_{1,\max}\approx466.7\,\text{N}\]
   Safe stress for segment \(Q\):
   \[\sigma_{w2}=\frac{4.5\times10^8}{3}=1.5\times10^8\,\text{Pa}\]
   Safe load for segment \(Q\):
   \[F_{2,\max}=\sigma_{w2}A_2\]

   \[F_{2,\max}=150\,\text{N}\]
   The series cable is limited by segment \(Q\), so:
   \[F_{\text{safe}}=150\,\text{N}\]
   Extension of segment \(P\):
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{FL_1}{A_1Y_1}\]
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{(150)(1.5)}{(2.0\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})}\,\text{m}\]
   \[\Delta L_1=\frac{225}{4.0\times10^5}\,\text{m}\]

   Extension of segment \(Q\):
   \[\Delta L_2=\frac{FL_2}{A_2Y_2}\]
